summary: Surveys implementations of BGP-4 that support the MIB agents defined in RFC 1657, according to the BGP-4 version 1 MIB specification. It is an informational record of which implementations support that management interface.

eli5.summary: A questionnaire sent to companies asking which of them have built a certain dashboard for their routers, and a list of who said yes.

questions: can you configure bgp through snmp
what bgp information can you read from snmp
do bgp implementations support snmp traps
subtitle: Survey of which BGP-4 router vendors support network management interfaces

tldr.problem: Network operators need to know which BGP-4 implementations support the management interface (MIB) defined in RFC 1657, and how completely each vendor implements it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4275 surveys three major router vendors (Cisco, NextHop, Redback) about their BGP-4 MIB implementations, including which management objects they support, write capabilities, notifications, and interoperability testing results.
tldr.outcome: The survey shows that all three vendors support core read-only management objects, but none support writing to configuration parameters, and notifications are inconsistently implemented across vendors.

today: RFC 4275 is an informational survey from 2006 documenting BGP-4 MIB implementation status. It remains a historical record of how vendors supported the management interface at that time. Modern BGP deployments have evolved, though the core MIB-based monitoring mechanisms continue to be used.

sections.title: Understanding BGP Management
sections.content: BGP routers at the edges of networks need to be monitored and managed. RFC 1657 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for BGP-4, a standardized set of data objects that operators can query and examine through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). These objects let network managers watch what BGP is doing: which peers are connected, how many routes are advertised, how often updates are sent, and whether errors have occurred. To understand how well this MIB is implemented in practice, RFC 4275 surveys three major router vendors: Cisco Systems, NextHop Technologies, and Redback Networks.
sections.eli5: Network managers use SNMP to ask routers 'What is BGP doing right now?' This document asks vendors 'Do you answer all the questions the specification says you should?'

sections.title: What the Survey Found
sections.content: All three vendors' implementations support the read-only management objects defined in the MIB. These include basic router information (BGP version, local AS number, router identifier), peer information (addresses, port numbers, AS numbers), counters for messages exchanged (UPDATE messages, total messages), and path attributes. However, the survey revealed gaps: none of the three implementations support write access to configuration parameters. These read-write objects in the MIB specification—such as bgpPeerAdminStatus, bgpPeerHoldTimeConfigured, and bgpPeerKeepAliveConfigured—cannot be modified through SNMP in any of the surveyed implementations. Additionally, support for notifications (also called traps in SNMP) is inconsistent. Cisco implements both bgpEstablished and bgpBackwardTransition notifications, but NextHop implements neither, and Redback implements only the backward transition notification (and only for the transition from Established to Idle state).
sections.eli5: Managers can watch the routers and see what they're doing, but they can't send commands to change how the routers work. Some routers will alert managers when something changes, but not all of them do.

sections.title: Detailed Findings and Counter Behavior
sections.content: The survey asked detailed questions about counter initialization and reset behavior. All three vendors initialize the counter objects bgpPeerInUpdates, bgpPeerOutUpdates, bgpPeerInTotalMessages, and bgpPeerOutTotalMessages to zero. However, when a configured peer enters the established state (meaning the BGP connection is up and working), the vendors handle counters differently. Cisco and NextHop do not reset the counters; they continue accumulating from their previous values. Only Redback resets these counters to zero when a peer becomes established. This difference could matter to network operators who use these counters to track BGP activity: different vendors will report different counter values for the same scenario.
sections.eli5: When a router starts tracking a BGP neighbor, vendors disagree on whether to reset the counters. Think of it like a fitness tracker: should it start counting steps from zero, or keep the old number?

sections.title: Interoperability and Implementation Details
sections.content: The survey included hands-on interoperability testing. Cisco tested with its internal management software but did not provide full details of all testing. NextHop uses an independent implementation and tested with UC Davis SNMP Tools (Net-SNMP) and Multi Router Traffic Grapher (MRTG), confirming read access to BGP-4 MIB variables works. NextHop provides agent access through the SNUX (SNMP Multiplex) interface. Redback's implementation is based on SNMP Research EMANATE code. All three implementations initialized counters to zero, and all show no interoperability problems between the manager and agent. For deprecated MIB objects from earlier BGP versions, vendors implement these differently but correctly handle the deprecation status.
sections.eli5: The vendors tested their implementations with real management software to make sure they work. They use different technologies under the hood but all ended up working without major problems.

sections.title: Implementation Status and Limitations
sections.content: The survey reveals both good news and limitations. The good news is that all three vendors support core BGP-4 MIB functionality for monitoring: operators can read virtually all the information they need to understand BGP peer status, route counts, and message activity. The limitations are noteworthy: no vendor allows remote SNMP configuration of BGP parameters, which means managers cannot use SNMP to change BGP behavior (they need other configuration channels). Notification support is spotty, meaning some monitoring systems cannot be automatically alerted when BGP state changes. These findings informed the industry that while BGP-4 MIB monitoring is standardized, vendors have not yet fully implemented all features the standard allows. This has not prevented widespread BGP deployment; instead, operators have adapted their practices to work with what is available and use other mechanisms for remote BGP configuration.
sections.eli5: The result: routers let you watch BGP, but not control it through the dashboard. If you want to change something, you have to log in another way.
